sections.skill: Explain the factors that affect credit scores and how scores affect borrowing costs

questions.prompt: In the widely used FICO model, which factor has the LARGEST weight?

choices.text: Payment history (about 35%)
Credit mix (about 10%)
New credit (about 10%)
Length of credit history (about 15%)

questions.intro: A credit score is a number (often 300–850) that summarizes credit risk based on a credit report. FICO's general weights: payment history about 35%, amounts owed about 30%, length of credit history about 15%, new credit about 10%, and credit mix about 10%. Other scoring models exist.
sources: myFICO (Fair Isaac Corporation): FICO score factor weights: payment history 35%, amounts owed 30%, length of credit history 15%, new credit 10%, credit mix 10%; scores range 300-850. (https://www.myfico.com/credit-education/whats-in-your-credit-score)

questions.prompt: Two applicants want a $20,000, 5-year car loan. Applicant A (strong credit) is offered 6% APR, with a $386.66 payment; Applicant B is offered 12% APR, with a $444.89 payment. How much more does B pay over 5 years?
questions.intro: Credit scores affect the interest rates lenders offer. A higher score usually means a lower rate, which lowers monthly payments and total cost.
sources: myFICO (Fair Isaac Corporation): FICO score factor weights: payment history 35%, amounts owed 30%, length of credit history 15%, new credit 10%, credit mix 10%; scores range 300-850. (https://www.myfico.com/credit-education/whats-in-your-credit-score)

questions.prompt: Which action is MOST likely to raise a credit score over time?

choices.text: Opening several new cards in one month
Maxing out a credit card
Paying every bill on time
Closing your oldest account

questions.intro: Scores reward on-time payments and low balances compared with limits, and can drop with late payments, high balances, and many new applications.
questions.feedback: Consistent on-time payments are the strongest positive factor.

questions.prompt: Ana and Ben have identical credit reports, but Ben earns twice as much. How do their FICO scores likely compare?

choices.text: Ben's is much higher
Ana's is higher because she borrows more of her income
They are about the same
Ben's is lower because higher earners spend more

questions.intro: Credit scores use only information in credit reports. Income, employment, savings, age, race, and where you live are not part of the score.
questions.feedback: Income is not in credit reports, so identical reports give about the same score (lenders may still ask about income).

misconceptions.A: Believes income is part of the score

questions.prompt: Ivy's FICO score is 780; Max's is 580. Which statement is MOST accurate?

choices.text: Max will pay lower rates, since lower is better
Both will get identical offers
Scores do not affect borrowing

questions.correct_answer: Max will likely face higher rates or denials
questions.feedback: On the 300–850 scale, higher scores indicate lower risk and usually get better terms.

questions.prompt: Maya's oldest card is 2 years old; her friend's is 15 years old. Both pay on time and owe little. Which score factor most likely favors her friend?

choices.text: Payment history
Amounts owed
Credit mix

questions.intro: FICO's five factors: payment history (paying on time), amounts owed (balances and utilization), length of credit history (age of accounts), new credit (recent applications), and credit mix (types of accounts).
questions.feedback: Older accounts help the length-of-history factor.

misconceptions.A: Both pay on time, so this does not separate them
misconceptions.C: Nothing says their account types differ

questions.prompt: A landlord checks Tia's credit before approving an apartment. Why?

choices.text: To predict whether she will pay rent on time
To see her school grades
To check her medical history and recent doctor visits
To learn her income

questions.correct_answer: To predict whether she will pay rent on time
questions.intro: Landlords often review credit reports or scores because past bill-paying predicts rent payment.
questions.feedback: Credit history helps landlords predict on-time rent.

questions.prompt: In many states, auto insurers use credit-based insurance scores. What does this mean for drivers with weaker credit?

choices.text: They pay lower premiums
They cannot buy insurance
They may pay higher premiums
Their driving record is ignored

questions.intro: Many insurers use credit-based insurance scores to help set prices, where state law allows.
questions.feedback: Weaker credit can raise premiums in states that allow this.

choices.text: Nothing; employers can check anyone
Tia must pay a fee
The employer must pay Tia's credit card bill
Tia must give written permission

questions.intro: Employers may review credit reports (not scores) for some jobs, but federal law requires your written permission. Some states limit this further.
questions.feedback: Written permission is required for employment checks.

questions.intro: Over long loans, a small rate difference adds up: extra cost = monthly difference × number of payments.

questions.prompt: Which statement about "credit scores" is MOST accurate?

choices.text: Different models give a person many scores
Everyone has one official score set by the government
Scores are updated only once a year
Scores are the same at every bureau

questions.correct_answer: Different models give a person many scores
questions.intro: FICO and VantageScore both make several versions, and each bureau's data differs, so scores vary.
questions.feedback: Different models and bureaus produce different scores.

misconceptions.C: Misses that scores change as reports change

questions.prompt: Myth or fact: "Checking my own credit report lowers my score."

choices.text: Fact: every check lowers your score
Fact: only on weekends
Myth: your own check is a soft inquiry
Fact: each check lowers your score by about 50 points

questions.correct_answer: Myth: your own check is a soft inquiry
questions.intro: Checking your own report or score is a soft inquiry and never affects scores.
questions.feedback: Self-checks are soft inquiries; check as often as you like.

Fact: scores need debt to exist

questions.correct_answer: Myth: paying in full still shows on-time use
questions.intro: Card use is reported each month. Paying the full statement balance shows responsible use without paying interest.
questions.feedback: You do not need to pay interest to build credit.

choices.text: Fact: fewer cards always means higher scores
Fact: closed cards are deleted immediately

questions.correct_answer: Myth: it can raise utilization and shorten history

questions.feedback: Closing a card can raise your utilization ratio and, over time, shorten your history.

misconceptions.B: Believes closed accounts vanish from reports
misconceptions.C: Believes closing an account removes its history

questions.prompt: Myth or fact: "Shopping for a car loan at several lenders within a short period ruins my score."

choices.text: Fact: each inquiry costs about 50 points every time
Myth: they usually count as one inquiry
Fact: you must never compare lenders
Fact: only the first lender counts

questions.correct_answer: Myth: they usually count as one inquiry
questions.intro: Scoring models usually treat multiple inquiries for the same kind of loan (car, mortgage, student) within a short window as one, so you can shop for the best rate.
questions.feedback: Rate shopping within a short window is generally treated as a single inquiry.
